{{Short description|American mathematics educator}}
{{About|the American mathematician|the fictional character in the British television crime drama|Peaky Blinders (TV series)}}
'''Bonnie Gold''' (born 1948){{r|born}} is an American mathematician, [[mathematical logic]]ian, [[philosophy of mathematics|philosopher of mathematics]], and [[mathematics education|mathematics educator]]. She is a [[Professor Emerita|professor emerita]] of mathematics at [[Monmouth University]].{{r|monmouth}}

==Education and career==
Gold completed her Ph.D. in 1976 at [[Cornell University]], under the supervision of [[Michael D. Morley]].{{r|mgp}}

She was the chair of the mathematics department at [[Wabash College]] before moving to Monmouth, where she also became department chair.{{r|prestigious}}

==Contributions==
The research from Gold's dissertation, ''Compact and <math>\omega</math>-compact formulas in <math>L_{\omega_{1},\omega}</math>'',{{r|mgp}}
was later published in the journal ''Archiv für Mathematische Logik und Grundlagenforschung'', and concerned [[infinitary logic]].{{r|nebres}}

With Sandra Z. Keith and William A. Marion she co-edited ''Assessment Practices in Undergraduate Mathematics'', published by the [[Mathematical Association of America]] (MAA) in 1999.{{r|lesser}}
With Roger A. Simons, Gold is also the editor of another book, ''Proof and Other Dilemmas: Mathematics and Philosophy'' (MAA, 2008).{{r|pod}}

Her essay "How your philosophy of mathematics impacts your teaching" was selected for inclusion in ''The Best Writing on Mathematics 2012''. In it, she argues that the [[philosophy of mathematics]] affects the teaching of mathematics even when the teacher's philosophical principles are implicit and unexamined.{{r|best}}

==Recognition==
In 2012, Gold became the winner of the 22nd [[Louise Hay Award]] of the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] for her contributions to [[mathematics education]]. The award citation noted her work in [[educational assessment]] for undergraduate study in mathematics.{{r|hay}}
